query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: HEA surface coatings, particularly CoCrFeNiMo0.85 applied via laser metal deposition, increase corrosion resistance of steels by promoting the formation of a uniform, adherent passivation layer enriched in Mo and Cr that blocks aggressive species from attacking the substrate.
generation.material_initial_state: Standard carbon or stainless steel substrates with typical native oxide layers and no specialized corrosion-resistant coatings.
generation.intervention: Application of high-entropy alloy coatings (e.g., CoCrFeNiMo0.85) using controlled laser metal deposition to produce defect-minimized surfaces.
generation.conditions: Laboratory simulation of aggressive chemical environments (e.g., saline solutions or simulated nuclear/chemical process fluids) at elevated temperatures relevant to chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, uniform HEA coating that develops a passivation film enriched in Mo and Cr, with minimal manufacturing defects and enhanced adhesion to the steel substrate.
generation.mechanism: The HEA coating facilitates selective oxidation and enrichment of Mo and Cr, forming stable oxide phases that effectively reduce metal dissolution. This passivation film serves as a physical and chemical barrier, lowering the corrosion current density compared to the uncoated base material.
generation.predicted_outcome: Steel specimens with the HEA coating will exhibit lower corrosion rates, reduced pit formation, and lower electrochemical corrosion current densities relative to uncoated steels under identical exposure conditions.
generation.baseline: Corrosion performance metrics (e.g., corrosion rate, pit density, current density) measured on uncoated steel substrates under the same environmental conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to steels used in environments typical of chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications. It may not hold if coating defects are prevalent or if the operational environment exceeds the chemical and thermal stability limits of the HEA coating.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent of the corrosion rate reduction and the exact composition of the passivation film may vary with processing parameters and environmental specifics, necessitating further experimental optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of steel samples: one set coated with CoCrFeNiMo0.85 HEA using laser metal deposition under optimized conditions, and a control set of uncoated steels. Expose both sets to a controlled corrosive environment (e.g., a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at elevated temperature) that simulates conditions in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications. Ensure that environmental parameters such as temperature, chloride concentration, and exposure time are identical for both sets.
measurements: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy to measure corrosion current densities
Surface morphological assessment via microscopy (e.g., SEM) to quantify pit formation and coating integrity
Chemical analysis (e.g., XPS) to determine the enrichment of Mo and Cr in the surface passivation film
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA-coated samples do not display a statistically significant improvement in corrosion resistance (i.e., similar corrosion current densities, pit formation, and passivation film composition) compared to the uncoated samples under the test conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.

AbstractGeothermal process equipment and accessories are usually manufactured from low-alloy steels which offer affordability but increase the susceptibility of the materials to corrosion. Applying erosion-corrosion-resistant coatings to these components could represent an economical solution to the problem. In this work, testing of two newly developed laser metal deposited high-entropy alloy (LMD-HEA) coatings—CoCrFeNiMo0.85 and Al0.5CoCrFeNi, applied to carbon and stainless steels—was carried out at the Hellisheidi geothermal power plant. Tests in three different geothermal environments were performed at the Hellisheidi site: wellhead test at 194 °C and 14 bar, erosion test at 198 °C and 15 bar, and aerated test at 90 °C and 1 bar. Post-test microstructural characterization was performed via Scanning Eletron Microscope (SEM), Back-Scattered Electrons analysis (BSE), Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS), optical microscopy, and optical profilometry while erosion assessment was carried out using an image and chemical analysis. Even if the Eoc has a more electronegative value than the bulk as-cast alloy [] the alloy developed rapidly a corrosion protection film and the corrosion current intensity was very small. The calculated corrosion rate is also very small indicating good corrosion behavior for the tested alloy.
